audit_scope.description: Trust model analysis for Ethereum EL/CL components based on EIP-140 (REVERT), Spurious Dragon fork specifications, EIP-6916 (testnet reset), Cancun memory operations, and EIP-7713 (box type encoding)

misclassified_entities.reason: Internal EVM component, not an external entity crossing trust boundary
Internal EVM opcode execution mechanism, not an external entity
Internal EVM bytecode interpreter, not an external entity

trusted_external_entities.name: Malicious Validator Operator
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Validator Deposit Contract / Beacon Chain Validator Registration
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External actor attempting to gain majority control of testnet validator set through mass validator deposits. This is an adversarial entity that must be defended against through mechanisms like EIP-6916's automatic reset cycle. The attacker has full network access and can deposit validators at any time, subject only to activation queue limits. Trust level is UNTRUSTED as this represents a threat actor in the security model.

trusted_external_entities.name: Decentralized Application
trusted_external_entities.rationale: External application constructing EIP-712 typed structured data messages with boxed values for user signatures. DApps interact with wallets to request signatures from users. These applications are untrusted as they can craft arbitrary signing requests, potentially malicious. The EL must validate all inputs from DApps and ensure proper encoding and hashing according to EIP-712 and EIP-7713 specifications. Users' wallets serve as the validation boundary.

trusted_external_entities.name: Wallet Software
trusted_external_entities.rationale: User wallet software that validates and displays EIP-712 signing requests before user approval. While wallets act as guardians for users, from the EL's perspective they are external entities that could be compromised or malicious. Wallets must validate box type schemas, check type isolation constraints, and render contents accurately. Classified as UNTRUSTED because the EL cannot assume wallet implementations are correct or non-malicious.

trusted_external_entities.name: User/Signer
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Human user reviewing and approving signing requests presented by wallet software. Users can be tricked by social engineering or phishing attacks into signing malicious transactions. From a technical trust model perspective, users are external to the EL system boundary and their actions cannot be assumed to be always correct or well-informed. The system must defend against user mistakes through clear UX and validation.

trusted_external_entities.name: Signing Contract
trusted_external_entities.entry_point: Smart Contract Execution Context / ECRECOVER precompile
trusted_external_entities.rationale: Smart contract on-chain that verifies EIP-712 signatures containing boxed values. These contracts are user-deployed code running on the EL and are external to the core EL implementation. Contracts interact with the EL through opcodes and precompiles (ECRECOVER) to verify signatures. Classified as UNTRUSTED because contract code can be arbitrary and potentially malicious, though it runs within the EVM's sandboxed environment.

boundary_edges.security_assumption: The CL must enforce activation queue rate limits (churn limit) to prevent rapid validator set takeover. EIP-6916 automatic reset mechanism must trigger before attacker can accumulate 66% majority. For 10k genesis validators, reset period must be < 5.7 days. The CL validates deposit signatures and pubkeys but cannot prevent economically-capable attackers from depositing validators.

DApp provides EIP-712 typed data message with boxed values. The wallet (not EL directly) validates message structure, type schema correctness, and type isolation. The EL only processes the final signed transaction/message. Security depends on wallet correctly implementing EIP-712/EIP-7713 validation before presenting to user. DApp can craft arbitrary messages but cannot forge signatures without user's private key.

Wallet must validate: (1) box structure has exactly three properties (value, primaryType, types), (2) inner type definitions follow EIP-712 rules, (3) inner types do not reference outer struct types (isolation constraint), (4) type hash computation follows specification. Wallet must render decoded box contents to user, not opaque hex. If wallet validation is bypassed or buggy, users could sign unintended commitments.

User reviews displayed message contents and approves signature. Security relies on: (1) wallet accurately displaying message contents including decoded box values, (2) user understanding what they are signing, (3) user's private key remaining secure. System assumes users can be socially engineered, so wallet UX must clearly present security-relevant information. User's signature commits them to the entire message including all boxed contents.

Contract calls ECRECOVER precompile to recover signer address from signature and message hash. The EL's ECRECOVER implementation must correctly implement secp256k1 signature recovery. Contract computes message hash according to EIP-712/EIP-7713, including proper box hash computation. Contract logic determines authorization (e.g., checking if recovered address matches expected signer). EL provides cryptographic primitive; authorization logic is contract's responsibility.

notes: All genuinely external entities have been identified with corresponding boundary edges
Three entities (EXT-TRANSACTION-EXECUTION, EXT-EVM-CREATE, EXT-EVM-INTERPRETER) were correctly reclassified as internal EL components
File spec_834c0eab895dcf9616a42e389ac43071bd019772.json (EIP-140 REVERT) contained no external entities - purely internal EVM state transitions
File spec_8c6f1d7d7517.json (Cancun memory operations) contained no external entities - internal EVM memory management
The trust model covers both adversarial actors (attacker) and regular system participants (DApps, wallets, users, contracts)
Trust boundaries properly distinguish between CL (validator management) and EL (transaction/contract execution) components
